analysis.one_liner: Makes voting easier, forces disclosure of political money, and tightens ethics rules for officials.
analysis.headline: The Senate's sweeping voting-rights and campaign-finance bill had 46 cosponsors, all Democrats and independents, but was never acted on by the Senate before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have overhauled how Americans vote and how campaigns are financed. It would have registered eligible voters automatically when they interact with government agencies, expanded early voting, voting by mail, and same-day registration, required paper ballots, and created independent commissions to draw congressional districts. On money in politics, it would have required groups spending on elections to disclose their donors, cracked down on foreign money, created a small-donor matching system for Senate candidates, and forced presidential candidates to release 10 years of tax returns. It also imposed new ethics rules on all three branches of government, including a code of conduct for federal judges and restrictions on the revolving door between government and industry.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters — especially young people, people with disabilities, racial and ethnic minorities, formerly incarcerated citizens, and people who move or have trouble taking time off work — would get automatic, online, and same-day registration, early voting, mail voting, and postage-paid ballots. Senate candidates who rely on small donations would get public matching funds, reducing their dependence on large donors. Voters would learn who is funding political ads and super PACs, and citizens would gain new tools to hold officeholders accountable through stricter ethics and disclosure rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters, small-donor candidates, and reform advocates

how_it_helps.text: The bill would require states to automatically register eligible citizens to vote using information from government agencies (motor vehicles, Social Security, Veterans Affairs, and others), unless the person declines.
It would require same-day voter registration, early voting, voting by mail, and postage-free ballots, and would restore voting rights to citizens after they finish a criminal sentence.
It would require voter-verified paper ballots, risk-limiting audits, and provide federal grants to states to secure their election systems.
It would require states to draw congressional districts with independent, nonpartisan commissions instead of letting legislators draw their own districts.
It would expand disclosure rules so organizations spending money on elections, campaign ads, and online platforms must reveal who is paying, and would expand the ban on foreign money in elections.
It would create an alternative campaign funding system for Senate elections in which the federal government matches small contributions from ordinary donors.

It would require a code of ethics for federal judges, bar senators from serving on for-profit boards, slow the revolving door between government and the private sector, and require presidential and vice-presidential candidates to submit 10 years of tax returns.
It would require Members of Congress to reimburse the Treasury for taxpayer-funded settlements in workplace harassment cases against them.

analysis.who_pays: Large donors, super PACs, and nonprofit groups that spend on politics without disclosing donors would lose their ability to operate in the dark. Lobbyists would face expanded disclosure requirements and stronger foreign-agent enforcement. States would bear compliance costs for new registration and voting procedures, though the bill authorizes federal grants to cover them. Taxpayers would fund the small-donor matching system and election security grants.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big donors, dark-money groups, lobbyists, and states

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes $500 million in grants for fiscal year 2019 plus 'such sums as may be necessary' in later years for automatic registration and election administration — a real ongoing cost to federal taxpayers.

It imposes federal mandates on all 50 states' election systems — automatic registration, early voting, mail voting, and paper ballots — overriding state-level choices about how to run elections, which critics saw as an unwarranted federal takeover.

Requiring broad disclosure of donors to organizations that spend on elections raises a good-faith objection that it could expose private citizens who support unpopular causes to public pressure, and it tightens lobbying rules that nonprofit advocacy groups also rely on.

The public financing and grant programs add new spending and administrative machinery — a national commission, a lobbying clearinghouse, new FEC structures — that honest critics would call an expansion of government.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefits — easier voting, transparent political money, and real ethics enforcement — are broad and durable, while the costs are mostly borne by groups and donors who now operate without disclosure, plus a meaningful but modest federal outlay for election infrastructure. The strongest honest objection is that federalizing election administration takes choices away from states and that forced donor disclosure carries privacy risks. On balance, the bill's costs are concentrated on politically powerful interests and its benefits are diffuse and democratic.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on day one, and then nothing happened — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote, for the entire two-year Congress.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Udall introduced the bill on March 28, 2019, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
The bill attracted 46 cosponsors — 44 Democrats and 2 independents — but no Republican cosponsors.
The full action history shows no further action of any kind after the committee referral: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
The House passed its companion version of this legislation (H.R. 1, the same For the People Act) in March 2019, but the Senate never took it up.

The bill's scope was enormous: it combined voter access, election security, campaign finance transparency, public financing of Senate races, and ethics rules for all three branches of government in a single bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent officeholders and organizations that spend heavily on politics without disclosure are better off, since none of the disclosure, public financing, redistricting, or ethics requirements ever took effect. State legislatures that draw their own congressional districts also kept that power.

for.name: Sen. Tom Udall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled a broad coalition of Senate cosponsors.

for.name: 46 Senate cosponsors (44 Democrats, 2 independents)
for.role: Cosponsors including party leadership, Sens. Schumer, Klobuchar, Durbin, and Warren
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it the Senate's flagship democracy reform measure of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for debate or a vote during the entire two-year Congress, calling it a partisan power grab.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-IA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing or markup — for the life of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 46 cosponsors were Democrats or independents and none was a Republican [S4]; the Senate Republican majority controlled the floor and committee calendars and never scheduled the bill for action [S5].

industries.industry: Big-money political spenders (super PACs, donor-advised dark-money nonprofits, foreign-linked money channels)
industries.note: The bill would force disclosure of who funds election spending, expand disclaimer rules to online ads, and widen the ban on foreign money — costs that fall only on interests that profit from undisclosed influence. Its interest runs against voters' interest in knowing who is trying to sway them.

Expanded lobbying disclosure, a dedicated Justice Department foreign-agent enforcement unit, and revolving-door restrictions would raise the cost and risk of influence-peddling. Their gain from blocking the bill is the public's loss of transparency.

industries.industry: Incumbent officeholders (Members of Congress, White House, executive officials)
industries.note: Tax return requirements, a judicial code of conduct, a ban on senators serving on for-profit boards, and forced reimbursement of taxpayer-funded harassment settlements all constrain officeholders themselves. Their interest in blocking it conflicts with public accountability.

industries.industry: Election technology and voting machine vendors
industries.note: Federal grants for paper-ballot systems, audits, and a requirement to use US-made voting machines would have created a funded market for compliant equipment. Voters and vendors both benefit from more secure systems.

Platforms would face political-ad record-keeping and disclaimer requirements, while broadcasters would have to offer discounted ad rates to participating candidates — new compliance burdens, offset in broadcast's case by ad revenue.
